content.text: Developers running DSO on nava-platform projects experience friction from accumulated codebase bloat that prevention gates cannot address retroactively. Specifically: false test failures from change-detector tests slow CI and erode trust in the test suite; stale documentation sections generate noise in code review; and dead code (unreachable branches, unused variables) slows codebase comprehension for new contributors. This epic adds a /dso:remediate skill that safely prunes high-confidence bloat patterns and surfaces lower-confidence candidates through an opus blue-team filter before presenting them for human resolution. The observable improvement: after running /dso:remediate --all, the developer sees a structured summary of what was cleaned, flagged, or skipped — and the next CI run, code review, and onboarding session encounters less noise.

Pattern namespace: bright-line patterns use category prefixes (T, D, C) and are eligible for auto-remediation. Probabilistic patterns use the P- prefix (P-T1, P-D3, P-C1) and are always routed to the blue-team agent when in confidence range — never auto-remediated regardless of threshold.

SC1. A new skill /dso:remediate is added, invoked with one of four scoped flags: --tests, --docs, --code, or --all. Invocation without a flag prints usage and exits non-zero. A sub-agent guard runs at skill entry: if the Agent tool is unavailable, the skill returns an error message and exits without mutations. Before any mutation, the skill checks for staged changes (git diff --cached --quiet); if staged changes exist, it aborts with an error.

SC2. A static confidence mapping file (YAML) ships with the plugin at plugins/dso/config/remediate-confidence-map.yaml, declaring {pattern_id, engine} -> confidence_score for every pattern/engine combination. Each per-stack linter (ruff, eslint, rubocop) has its own engine entry. Two new dso-config.conf keys control routing: remediate.auto_threshold (default: 90) and remediate.blue_team_threshold (default: 60). At runtime, the skill detects installed engines via command -v, looks up the highest-confidence installed engine for each pattern, and routes: >= auto_threshold -> auto-remediate, >= blue_team_threshold -> route to blue-team agent, < blue_team_threshold -> skip with a note in the summary.
SC3. The skill detects and auto-remediates the following bright-line patterns when confidence meets the auto threshold:
- --tests: T1 (assertion-less test body — auto-delete the test function), T2 (exact-duplicate test — auto-delete the duplicate), T3 (import-only test file — auto-delete the file)

- --docs: D2 (broken internal links — annotate with TODO: fix or remove inline comment), D4 (duplicate headings — included in summary as flagged_for_review with file path), D5 (large unstructured file — included in summary as flagged_for_review with file path)

- --code: C1 (unreachable branch after unconditional return/raise/throw — auto-delete the dead block), C2 (unused local variable without suppression annotation — auto-delete), C3 (exact-duplicate function body — included in summary as flagged_for_review with both file paths)

For C2, auto-prune is suppressed if the line contains # noqa, # type: ignore, or # side-effect; such matches are flagged for human review instead. For C1 and C2, the skill delegates to per-stack linters when available, falling back to semgrep rules.

SC4. For probabilistic patterns where the best available engine's confidence falls between the two thresholds, the skill dispatches a dso:bloat-blue-team opus sub-agent. Engine selection follows the same rule as SC2: the highest-confidence installed engine determines the routing decision. The blue-team agent emits one of three verdicts per candidate: CONFIRM, DISMISS (with rationale), or NEEDS_HUMAN (with ambiguity note). DISMISS candidates are excluded from the user-facing report. CONFIRM and NEEDS_HUMAN candidates both proceed to SC5 resolution paths. NEEDS_HUMAN is counted as a distinct field in the SC6 summary. Probabilistic patterns: P-T1 (change-detector test), P-D3 (stale example referencing absent symbol), P-C1 (feature flag never toggled to true). If no installed engine covers a probabilistic pattern, it is skipped and recorded in skipped_pattern_ids.
SC5. After blue-team filtering, the skill presents the user with a choice of two resolution paths:

- Path A (manual): Displays a numbered list of CONFIRM and NEEDS_HUMAN candidates with file location, pattern ID, and blue-team note. User enters item numbers to remove (comma-separated), or presses Enter to skip all. Fixture tests simulate Path A by injecting a pre-set selection list via DSO_REMEDIATE_SELECT env var.

- Path B (auto-resolve): Dispatches a dso:bloat-resolver opus sub-agent that applies all CONFIRM candidates and emits NO_CHANGE: <reason> for any it declines. Changes from the resolver follow the normal commit workflow (COMMIT-WORKFLOW.md -> /dso:review), ensuring at least two independent agents review every change.

SC6. The skill emits a structured session-end summary written to $ARTIFACTS_DIR/remediate-summary-<timestamp>.json with schema: {"auto_remediated": 0, "blue_team_dismissed": 0, "blue_team_needs_human": 0, "skipped_below_threshold": 0, "skipped_pattern_ids": [], "flagged_for_review": 0, "user_resolved": 0, "resolver_applied": 0, "resolver_no_change": 0, "flags": ["--tests"]}

SC7. Validation is run against each nava-platform template (flask, nextjs, rails, jekyll-uswds) using synthetic test fixtures at tests/fixtures/remediate/<template>/. Each fixture includes a fixture-manifest.json declaring expected counts and file-level outcomes. Validation asserts: auto-remediated items -> target file/function absent and auto_remediated count matches; flagged items -> no mutation and flagged_for_review count matches; skipped items -> skipped_pattern_ids contains expected IDs. Each fixture also includes at least one valid-but-pattern-matching item (e.g., intentional golden-file test, changelog with duplicate headings) that must NOT be removed — the manifest declares these as expected_false_positive_safe and the test asserts they remain unmodified.
Out of scope: P-D4 (concept drift), P-D1 (orphaned sections), P-T2 (mock-heavy tests), P-C2 (redundant parameters). These are deferred to follow-on epic bc7f-1a0d.
- P-T1 golden-file false positives (critical): Intentional regression tests are structurally identical to change-detectors; the static confidence mapping cannot distinguish them by project context.
- P-C1 env-flag false positives (critical): Feature flags gated on environment variables are statically never true during analysis, matching every env-conditional flag.
- auto_threshold=0 bypass (critical): Setting threshold to 0 routes all matches to auto-prune, bypassing blue-team entirely.
- Unbounded resolver batch (important): 50+ auto-prune candidates in a single dispatch may exhaust agent context.
- Test coverage gap after deletion (important): Deleting the sole test covering a source file leaves an invisible coverage gap.
- Interrupted mid-batch state (important): No checkpoint/state file to resume from after SIGURG.
- Inverted thresholds dead zone (important): blue_team_threshold > auto_threshold creates undefined routing behavior.
- Missing config key (important): Absent threshold keys cause bash comparison failure and silent abort.
- Stack-detection mismatch (important): Monorepo stack detection may select wrong linter for confidence lookup.
- Blue-team agent must form its verdict before consulting the engine confidence score to avoid anchoring
- Blue-team should default to DISMISS when uncertain — false CONFIRMs are amplified by the resolver; false DISMISSes are recoverable
- Resolver prompt must NOT mention the downstream review gate — prevents moral hazard
- Resolver must check for callers before deleting any function/class/export and emit NO_CHANGE with CASCADE_RISK when callers exist outside the candidate list
- Embed these as hard constraints in agent definition files during implementation

- Polyglot Piranha (Uber, https://github.com/uber/piranha): Java/Kotlin/Swift/ObjC/JS/Go. Tree-sitter AST with cascading cleanup rules. Auto-remediates (210K lines deleted, 1611 PRs). Binary match/no-match — no confidence tiering. Excels at feature flag cascading cleanup.
- DCE-LLM (NAACL 2025, https://aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-long.501/): Hybrid CodeBERT triage + LLM judgment. 94%+ F1. Architecturally closest to our approach but requires fine-tuned models.
- Knip (https://github.com/webpro-nl/knip): JS/TS only. TypeScript type checker as ground truth. Highest-precision JS/TS dead code detector — candidate linter delegate for JS/TS stack.
- Semgrep autofix (https://semgrep.dev/docs/writing-rules/autofix): 20+ languages. Rule-based or LLM-assisted (https://choly.ca/post/semgrep-autofix-llm/). No native confidence tiering.
- Datadog: LLM false-positive filtering for static analysis (https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/using-llms-to-filter-out-false-positives/)
- lychee (https://github.com/lycheeverse/lychee): Async Rust link checker. Fast, caching, .lycheeignore. Report only.
- markdownlint (https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint): MD024 duplicate headings with siblings_only option (changelog-aware). Has auto-fix. More precise than bash-grep for D4.
- Doc Detective (https://github.com/doc-detective): Execution-based stale example detection (runs docs against live system). Complementary to LLM approach.
- Vale (https://github.com/errata-ai/vale): Prose style linter with YAML rules. Can approximate P-D3 with deprecated-term lists but brittle vs LLM approach.
- TSDetect (https://github.com/TestSmells/TSDetect): Java only. 20 test smells including assertion-less (Unknown Test). Report only.
- TestIQ (https://github.com/pydevtools/TestIQ): Python/pytest. Coverage-based duplicate detection. Higher FP rate than AST hashing.

- UTRefactor (FSE 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.16739): Java. LLM-based auto-refactoring of test smells (89% reduction). Closest to our blue-team filter but collapses detection and remediation into one pass.
- Mutation testing (PIT, mutmut): Ground truth for test redundancy but too slow for commit gates.

No existing tool implements all three of our architectural pillars: per-pattern confidence mapping, tiered routing (auto/LLM/skip), and per-stack linter delegation. Implementation should consider: Knip as JS/TS linter delegate, markdownlint for D4 (siblings_only precision), Piranha's cascading pattern for resolver design.

No blocking epic dependencies. The confidence mapping YAML (plugins/dso/config/remediate-confidence-map.yaml) is a deliverable artifact — its schema is a stable interface that follow-on epic bc7f-1a0d will consume. Two new dso-config.conf entries: remediate.auto_threshold, remediate.blue_team_threshold. Runtime tool availability handled by confidence mapping graceful degradation.

Option A: Tiered Engine Selection. Ship a static confidence mapping YAML declaring {pattern_id, engine} -> confidence_score. At runtime, detect available engines via command -v, look up the highest-confidence available engine for each pattern, and route through three tiers using two global config thresholds. Detection engines: semgrep (declarative AST rules, polyglot), ast-grep (structural queries), bash-grep (textual fallback), plus delegation to per-stack linters (ruff, eslint, rubocop) where they already detect the pattern.
**dso:bloat-blue-team input**: {candidates: [{candidate_id, pattern_id, file, line_range, excerpt, engine, confidence}]}
- rationale required for DISMISS and NEEDS_HUMAN, optional for CONFIRM
- action enum: delete_function | delete_file | delete_block | annotate | flag
- no_change.category enum: CASCADE_RISK | INSUFFICIENT_CONTEXT | PATTERN_UNCLEAR | STACK_UNCERTAINTY (required)

Add to SC2: If either config key (remediate.auto_threshold, remediate.blue_team_threshold) is absent, non-numeric, or outside 1-100, log warning to stderr naming the invalid key and value, then use defaults (auto=90, blue_team=60) for the entire run. If blue_team_threshold >= auto_threshold after resolution, log warning (inverted thresholds) but proceed.

Add to SC2: At scan start, classify files in scope into language groups by extension. For each language group, select the highest-confidence installed engine. Extension-to-language mapping is a static lookup table shipped alongside the confidence mapping YAML. Unrecognized extensions scanned with bash-grep only.
Blue-team: form verdict before consulting confidence; default to DISMISS when uncertain; 80%+ definitive rate; declare rationale_basis.
Resolver: no mention of downstream review gate; check callers before deleting; categorize every NO_CHANGE.

SC3 ACHIEVABLE on all 4 stacks. Confidence ranges: Python python-ast 95, semgrep 85; JS/TS ast-grep 88; Ruby ast-grep 85; Markdown bash-grep 90. Ruby C1 lower confidence — consider routing to blue-team.

content.text: ## Pattern observed on PR #93 (small alias-backfill PR, 8 files)

The llm-review reviewer produced **three invalid critical-severity findings** across four review cycles on a ~150-line PR. Each invalid finding cost a fix/defend cycle, blocking merge and burning the autonomous-resolution budget on hallucinations. The valid findings on the same PR were legitimate and useful — but mixed with confident-sounding criticals that don't survive a manual trace.
This bug is about the **reviewer prompt/process**, not the individual findings. The findings themselves are now defended; the goal is to prevent the next PR from hitting the same pattern.

> \"plugins/dso/scripts/ticket_reducer/_alias.py computes os.path.join(here, '..', '..', 'resources', ...) which resolves to plugins/resources/ticket-wordlist.txt instead of plugins/dso/resources/ticket-wordlist.txt. The path should use only one '..'\"
The path is correct. The reviewer mis-counted \`..\` levels.
**Cycle 4, Finding 1 (critical) — claimed cross-implementation divergence on 8-hex IDs**

> \"ticket-alias-compute.py always computes a 3-word alias (adj-noun1-noun2) using hex[8:12] even when that range is out of bounds for 8-hex IDs. ticket_reducer/_alias.py correctly returns a 2-word alias.\"
The claim is that a ticket created with one alias would resolve to a different alias later. Tracing the actual callers:
- \`ticket-alias-compute.py\` is invoked only from \`ticket-create.sh\` / \`ticket_create\` in ticket-lib-api.sh
- Both creation paths generate 16-hex IDs via \`uuid.uuid4()\` — never 8-hex
- 8-hex IDs exist only on legacy tickets predating the alias feature; they reach aliases exclusively through read-time backfill in \`_alias.compute_alias\`
The divergence scenario cannot occur. The reviewer didn't trace which callers actually pass which input shapes.
> \"If the conditional were inverted to 'if NOT stored_alias:', this test would still pass.\"
Tracing the test against the inverted conditional:

The test does distinguish the two branches. The reviewer either didn't simulate the inverted code or simulated it incorrectly. The test also includes an explicit \`assert stored != backfill_would_yield\` invariant guarding exactly this property — the reviewer didn't mention that line.
All three invalid findings share specific failure modes:

1. **No call-graph trace before claiming divergence/crash**. The reviewer constructs a scenario (\"a legacy ticket created on a system where X...\") without verifying that any caller actually produces the inputs needed to reach that scenario. C1-F1 and C4-F1 both hallucinate code paths that don't exist.

2. **No counter-example simulation when claiming a test is tautological**. C4-F2 asserts the test would pass under a code mutation that, when actually simulated, makes the test fail. The reviewer skipped the mutation-test step that would have caught its own claim.

3. **No arithmetic verification for path/index counts**. C1-F1 mis-counted \`..\` levels in an \`os.path.join\`. Mechanical claims like 'this path resolves to X' are cheap to verify and the reviewer didn't.

4. **Critical severity inflation**. All three invalid findings were marked critical (severity 1-2), meaning CLAUDE.md R11 forbids overriding them and the autonomous loop must fix-or-defend each. Combined with the rate of invalidity (3 invalid criticals on one small PR), the cap of 5 resolution attempts (now 3) is consumed almost entirely by hallucinations.
The fix is not in the workflow code — it is in \`plugins/dso/scripts/dso_ci_review/\` reviewer prompts and the agent definitions in \`plugins/dso/agents/dso-code-reviewer-*.md\`. Candidates:

- **Pre-finding self-check**: before marking a finding critical, require the reviewer to (a) name the specific caller(s) that produce the input shape it claims is problematic, or (b) explicitly note that the code path is unreachable in current flow and downgrade severity.

- **Inverted-code simulation for tautology claims**: when claiming a test would pass under an inverted conditional, require the reviewer to print the value the test would actually assert under the mutation, then check whether the recorded assertion equals that value.

- **Path arithmetic check**: when claiming a relative path resolves incorrectly, require the reviewer to enumerate the directory components walked. This is mechanical and the reviewer is the one party that benefits from being forced to do it.

- **Severity calibration prompt**: a one-line rule — \"if the scenario described requires inputs the production callers cannot produce, downgrade from critical to important and tag the scenario as defensive-only.\"

- **Reuse of prior defenses**: per the defenses contract, cycle-N reviews should consume defense records before re-raising the same finding. Cycle 1 F1 reappeared verbatim in cycles 2, 3, 4 even after I addressed adjacent concerns — the DefenseStore lookup either isn't happening or isn't influencing the reviewer's output.
- Defense comment for C4-F1 and C4-F2: https://github.com/navapbc/digital-service-orchestra/pull/93#issuecomment-4426917563
- Counter-cited evidence: the four cycle-N comment threads on PR #93
### Out of scope for this ticket

Fixing the cited findings. They're already either fixed or defended on PR #93. The remediation here lives in the reviewer's prompt and the autonomous-loop control flow, not in the alias backfill code.

content.text: * **CI workflow:** Script Tests job on PR #94 (run 25710603591)
* **CI environment:** ubuntu-latest, Python 3.13.13 (per workflow env vars)
CI Script Tests job runs tests/scripts/test-merge-to-main.sh deterministically — same commit, same test, same result.
First CI run on PR #94 commit 99a068dcd2: 3 tests in tests/scripts/test-merge-to-main.sh FAILED with 'python parse error':
Rerun of the SAME job on the SAME commit (no code change): all 3 tests PASSED.
The same tests pass locally on macOS (PASSED: 69 FAILED: 0) and pass on main on adjacent runs (most recent main runs all show Script Tests conclusion=success).
#### Failure log excerpt from the failed run

The literal 'FAIL: python parse error' appears in the actual-value position of the assertion, indicating the test's helper python invocation returned 'parse error' instead of a parseable value. This suggests a runtime / parallelism / state issue in CI (e.g., temp-file race with another test running in parallel, locale-dependent JSON write, or stdin handling).
1. PR #94 opened (commit 99a068dcd2) — Script Tests failed at 6m37s.
2. Local reproduction attempted via 'bash tests/scripts/test-merge-to-main.sh' — PASSED 69/0.
3. Adjacent main runs all green for Script Tests.
5. Rerun of Script Tests on the same commit: PASSED 5m45s.

Same commit, same job, two different outcomes. Tests pass locally. Failure mode is reproducible in CI only intermittently. The 'FAIL: python parse error' string suggests a python helper in the test (or one of its dependencies) is sometimes returning unexpected stdout that does not parse as JSON or whatever schema the assertion expects.
Hypothesis directions (Zero Inference — directions only, no prescribed fix):

* Parallel test execution race: the failing tests likely write/read shared state (state file paths in test-merge-to-main.sh's _state_init / _state_write_phase / _state_mark_complete). If two parallel test files use overlapping state file paths in CI's parallelism, one could read another's partial write.
* CI-specific environment difference: Python 3.13.13 on ubuntu vs developer macOS; locale or JSON-handling differences could surface intermittently.

* Stdin / stdout handling in test helper: if a 'python -c' helper reads from stdin and stdin contains stale data (from a parallel test's pipe), parse failure on the empty/partial input would produce the observed 'parse error' result.
* Inspect the three failing tests for shared state (file paths, env vars) that might race with parallel test execution.
* Audit any 'python -c' / 'python3 -c' helper invocations in tests/scripts/test-merge-to-main.sh for stdin handling — confirm explicit /dev/null redirection where stdin should be empty.
* Add a retry-on-parse-error wrapper if the parse error is genuinely transient (last-resort mitigation; structural fix preferred).
* Consider whether these tests should opt into serial-only execution (skip the parallel test-runner queue) if the underlying state-file pattern fundamentally races.

content.text: The six calibration-program epics (a03c-d55e Closure Checks; 94ed-f55c plan-time intent allocation; d566-afa6 Tier 1+2 gen-time prevention; 7f42-e41f suite growth metrics; 69e8-af39 bug/review feedback loop; 411b-a047 mutation infrastructure Tier 3; 4911-c7ba bug-type taxonomy) produce per-event measurement signals — reviewer findings, intent coverage, mutation kill rates, negative-example extractions, graduation telemetry — but no aggregation layer. The headline program-success question — "what fraction of bugs are caught by tests vs review vs production, and is the ratio improving?" — is unanswerable today because bug tickets carry no detection-channel attribution and per-event data is never rolled up. The maintainer (sole stakeholder for the test-writing system in this repo) needs a measurement substrate to evaluate whether the system is improving over time. Without this epic, the six calibration epics ship infrastructure that delivers value but the maintainer cannot tell if it's working; the cost of the gap is silent regression — the system could degrade without anyone noticing.

This epic ships in two milestones back-to-back. Milestone 1 adds a detected_by:<channel> tag to bug tickets with seven allowed values (tests, review-llm, review-human, production, user-report, internal-dogfood, other); required for CLI_user-tagged bugs via the create-bug dialogue; auto-set via infer-detected-by.sh for the three agent filing paths (411b mutation auto-bug, /dso:fix-bug Phase G, debug-everything) based on filing context, defaulting to other when context is insufficient. No backfill — closed bugs remain other; time-series starts from M1 ship date. Milestone 2 builds the rollup tooling: a single plugins/dso/scripts/calibration-report.sh with subcommands (monthly, quarterly, mutation-append, churn-append, query <sub>); a thin /dso:test-quality-report skill wraps it for manual invocation; .github/workflows/calibration-rollup.yml runs per-PR mutation-append + churn-append and cron monthly + quarterly; rollup comments are posted via the ticket CLI to three tracking tickets (calibration-program-health, mutation-history, suite-churn-history). Hybrid data sourcing: mutation findings and suite-churn pre-aggregated per-PR; bug counts and reviewer-finding rates queried on demand. Rule-effectiveness measurement folds into the monthly rollup using promoted-to-standard:* tags + detected_by + bug-type-<slug> from 4911-c7ba.

Tickets-as-storage pattern throughout — rollups accumulate as comments on dedicated tracking tickets so they remain searchable via the ticket CLI, consistent with the rest of the calibration program's storage choices.

1. (M1) Bug tickets carry a detected_by:<channel> tag from the seven allowed values (tests, review-llm, review-human, production, user-report, internal-dogfood, other); create-bug dialogue prompts the human filer when the bug is CLI_user-tagged; infer-detected-by.sh sets the value from filing context for 411b mutation auto-bug, /dso:fix-bug Phase G, and debug-everything paths, defaulting to other when context is insufficient. Verified by unit tests covering each helper branch and an integration test for the CLI_user dialogue path. The helper is committed with the executable bit set and includes a self-test guard that fails CI if the binary is non-executable.

2. (M1) plugins/dso/skills/shared/prompts/bug-report-template.md and plugins/dso/skills/create-bug/SKILL.md document the detected_by field and its allowed values; .claude/scripts/dso ticket list --has-tag=detected_by:tests returns only bug-type tickets filed at or after M1 ship date (non-bug tickets that accidentally carry the tag do not appear in the result).

3. (M2) plugins/dso/scripts/calibration-report.sh supports subcommands monthly, quarterly, mutation-append, churn-append, and query <sub> (with sub values: intents-with-low-kill-rate, intents-without-coverage, bugs-by-channel-and-type, rule-effectiveness <rule-id>); each subcommand produces output matching its documented schema for a dry-run input fixture; the script is idempotent on repeated invocation for the same period (does not post duplicate comments).

4. (M2) Given a synthetic ticket fixture with a known detected_by distribution (e.g., 3 detected_by:tests, 2 detected_by:review-llm, 1 detected_by:production, 2 detected_by:other), calibration-report.sh monthly returns channel counts that exactly match the fixture. This fixture-driven correctness test runs in CI via calibration-rollup.yml before any append step and is also invoked as part of the M2 release gate locally.
5. (M2) /dso:test-quality-report skill is registered, invokes calibration-report.sh, and surfaces monthly and quarterly rollup outputs for manual invocation.

6. (M2) .github/workflows/calibration-rollup.yml runs mutation-append and churn-append on PR-merge events (with a per-PR append safeguard — advisory lock on the tracking ticket or post-append verification — so concurrent fast-follow PR merges produce neither duplicates nor lost entries) and runs monthly + quarterly on cron triggers using a single declared timezone (UTC) that the aggregation logic also uses for bucket boundaries; CI dry-run posts the expected comment shape to a test ticket; the workflow surfaces a non-zero exit and CI failure (not a silent skip) when calibration-report.sh fails or when a target tracking ticket is missing.

7. **SC7 (self-use, Probe-1 remediation, architecture-vs-evidence audit 2026-05-16):** Bugs filed during the a34c sprint exercise the calibration-channel attribution end-to-end before sprint close. At least one bug filed during the a34c sprint (via `/dso:create-bug`, sub-agent, or debug path) carries a valid `detected_by:<channel>` tag from the seven allowed values, AND `calibration-report.sh monthly` (run against a synthetic fixture or the in-flight ticket set) returns a non-empty channel breakdown that includes the just-filed bug's channel.

- `.claude/scripts/dso ticket list --type=bug --format=llm | python3 -c "import json,sys; ts=json.load(sys.stdin); print(sum(1 for t in ts for tag in (t.get('tags') or []) if tag.startswith('detected_by:')))"` returns ≥1.
- `plugins/dso/scripts/calibration-report.sh monthly --fixture=tests/fixtures/a34c-sprint-bugs` returns exit 0 with a `bugs-by-channel` section containing ≥1 entry.
Surviving scenarios after Red/Blue Team filter — these are design constraints for preplanning task decomposition, not separate SCs.
- CLI_user bug filed without detected_by prompt produces silent schema gap (high) — needs CLI-level enforcement, not just SKILL.md guidance.
- infer-detected-by.sh ambiguous-context path silently mis-tags when filing context is misleading (high) — e.g., human runs /dso:fix-bug on a production bug; filing context looks like review-llm.
- Duplicate detected_by tags on same ticket produce double-counting (medium) — calibration-report.sh must deduplicate.
- detected_by tag applied to non-bug tickets contaminates channel query (medium) — queries must filter by ticket type.
- Comment thread exceeds ticket CLI performance threshold at year 2+ (high) — known SIGURG scaling pattern (bug 2f20-eb16) not yet evaluated for single-ticket comment depth.
- calibration-report.sh scans full comment history rather than using a cursor (high) — linear query cost growth.
- No compaction or archival strategy (medium) — comments are permanent; mutation-history grows indefinitely.
- mutation-append races with fast-follow PR merges (critical) — ticket CLI append not described as atomic across concurrent writers.
- Skipped or failed mutation-append leaves invisible gap (critical) — no retry/alerting; unrecoverable past GHA's 90-day retention.
- On-demand reviewer-findings query reads tickets-branch at stale ref (high) — GHA cached workspace may miss recent findings.
- Month-boundary cron in UTC misaligns with bug-timestamp local time (high) — unify timezone across cron and aggregation.
- Double-run on cron + manual workflow_dispatch produces duplicate comment (medium) — needs idempotency check.
- GHA cron skipped run leaves permanent gap with no alerting (high) — trend queries silently bridge missing periods.
- Three tracking tickets must pre-exist before first CI run (high) — needs bootstrap/create-if-missing guard.
- calibration-rollup.yml referencing absent calibration-report.sh on PR merges (high) — workflow must guard for script existence or M1/M2 ship-order must enforce co-arrival.
- infer-detected-by.sh non-executable causes silent fallthrough to 'other' (high) — CLAUDE.md rule 11 + the self-test guard in SC1 mitigates.

| `detected_by:<channel>` tag (7 allowed values) | SC1: `/dso:create-bug` dialogue when CLI_user-tagged; `infer-detected-by.sh` for 411b auto-bug + Phase G + debug-everything paths; default `:other` | Stable (no mutation) | SC3 calibration-report.sh aggregation; downstream 69e8 / 411b / 4911 consumers | Implicit with bug ticket lifecycle; persists on closed tickets as historical attribution record |

| Tracking ticket `calibration-program-health` | Bootstrap guard per SC6 (workflow fails CI if missing); created once at epic ship | SC3 monthly/quarterly append subcommands | calibration-report.sh queries; manual review via /dso:test-quality-report | N/A — persistent by design. Comment thread is intentional append-only historical record per event-sourced ticket-system v3 semantics. Converts the audit's "no compaction" gap into a documented design choice. |

| Tracking ticket `mutation-history` | Same as `calibration-program-health` | SC6 mutation-append on PR-merge | calibration-report.sh `query intents-with-low-kill-rate` | Same as `calibration-program-health` |
| Tracking ticket `suite-churn-history` | Same | SC6 churn-append on PR-merge | calibration-report.sh `query rule-effectiveness` | Same |

| Per-PR append safeguard (advisory lock or post-append verification) | Per SC6 — chosen mechanism declared in calibration-rollup.yml | Each PR-merge run acquires/releases | The append job itself | Implicit per workflow run; lock is short-lived, released by workflow exit |
- `.claude/scripts/dso ticket exists calibration-program-health && .claude/scripts/dso ticket exists mutation-history && .claude/scripts/dso ticket exists suite-churn-history` returns 0.
- `grep -n 'advisory.*lock\|post-append verification' plugins/dso/workflows/calibration-rollup.yml` confirms the chosen safeguard is declared.
Closes the audit's named gap: tracking-ticket RETIRE = "N/A — persistent by design" (append-only historical record per ticket-system v3 semantics).
The original 2026-05-16 pass deferred probe 6. The session-completability rule treats gh CLI + ticket-CLI as in-session-verifiable. Adding the structured block:

| Three tracking tickets exist | `.claude/scripts/dso ticket exists calibration-program-health && .claude/scripts/dso ticket exists mutation-history && .claude/scripts/dso ticket exists suite-churn-history` | Returns 0 (all three present) |
| calibration-rollup.yml is active | `gh workflow list --json name,state \| jq '[.[] \| select(.name == "calibration-rollup") \| select(.state == "active")] \| length'` | ≥1 |

| Cron expression is valid + scheduled | `gh workflow view calibration-rollup.yml --yaml \| grep -E '^\s+- cron:'` | Returns ≥1 cron line; expression parses (no GHA validation error in `gh workflow view`) |

| Recent run succeeded (cron reliability indicator) | `gh run list --workflow=calibration-rollup.yml --limit=10 --json conclusion --jq '[.[] \| select(.conclusion == "success")] \| length'` | ≥1 in the last 10 runs; if zero, sprint surfaces the gap and operator decides (force-trigger or defer epic close) |

| Branch protection includes calibration check | `gh api /repos/$OWNER/$REPO/branches/main/protection 2>/dev/null \| jq '.required_status_checks.contexts // [] \| length'` | ≥0 — branch protection is OPTIONAL; documented posture either way |

| Workflow surfaces non-zero exit when tracking ticket missing (SC6) | Synthetic test: rename one tracking ticket via `dso ticket edit --title=...test-rename`, trigger workflow, assert run conclusion != success; restore name; verify rerun succeeds | Test pass before sprint close |

Converts the audit's prose-only external dependencies (GHA cron + tracking-ticket bootstrap + branch protection) into structured in-session checks. Cron-skipped-run-without-alerting remains a residual operational risk; the "recent run succeeded in last 10" check surfaces it before sprint closure rather than deferring entirely.
Soft consumers (this epic consumes their outputs; no hard blocking for design):
- 69e8-af39 — retro graduation telemetry; consumes detected_by as candidate-weighting signal from this epic
- 411b-a047 — per-PR mutation kill rates; auto-files mutation-breach bugs (will set detected_by:tests once this epic ships)
- 4911-c7ba — bug-type-<slug> taxonomy joined with detected_by:<channel> for cross-classification reporting
- M2 core script + skill is independently mergeable before the GHA workflow; the workflow ships as a follow-on task within the same milestone to reduce blast radius on CI iteration.

- M1 must merge before the 411b auto-bug pathway is activated; coordinate with 411b implementation to add detected_by:tests to infer-detected-by.sh output prior to 411b going live (coordination comment already on 411b-a047).
- M1 ship triggers a notification to 69e8-af39 so its graduation candidate-weighting can begin using detected_by; 69e8 must not hardcode a fallback that silently ignores the tag.
- Test-caught-regression event tagging from CI logs (Gap G) — deferred P3+ follow-on per user direction.
- Custom dashboards / web UI — surface is ticket comments + script output.
- Real-time streaming metrics — periodic rollups only.
- Backfill of detected_by on closed bugs — time-series starts from M1 ship date.
- Operational meta-criterion (e.g., "first non-degenerate rollup posted") — relying on per-deliverable SCs.
- Ticket comments on 411b-a047-18de-4516: its auto-bug-creation logic should set detected_by:tests when this epic ships.
- Ticket comments on 69e8-af39-7886-4ee9: its graduation phase can use detected_by as a candidate-weighting signal once this epic ships.
- Ticket comments on 4911-c7ba (via the now-closed cf65-e3b4-0bea-4756 story): detection-CHANNEL is a separate dimension from 4911's bug-TYPE taxonomy.
- cf65-e3b4-0bea-4756 closure comment recorded the re-parenting rationale.
Approach chosen: Option A — single shell script with thin skill wrapper, ticket-CLI-native.
1. Phased delivery: M1 detected_by first, M2 rollup back-to-back.
2. Rollup cadence: scheduled monthly + quarterly via GHA cron.
3. detected_by enforcement: required for CLI_user-tagged bugs; agent-filed bugs auto-set via infer-detected-by.sh based on filing context, default 'other'.
5. Tracking tickets: three (calibration-program-health, mutation-history, suite-churn-history); no yearly partitioning.
6. Aggregation timing: hybrid — pre-aggregate mutation+churn per-PR; query bugs+reviews on demand.
7. Meta-criterion: skipped; per-deliverable SCs suffice (with the fixture-driven correctness SC added during fidelity review).
1. At least one bug from the a34c sprint carries a valid detected_by:<channel> tag from the seven allowed values (tests, review-llm, review-human, production, user-report, internal-dogfood, other).
2. calibration-report.sh monthly --fixture=tests/fixtures/a34c-sprint-bugs returns exit 0 with a non-empty bugs-by-channel section.

content.text: The ticket CLI accepts short ID prefixes (e.g. \`f61f-7e0a\`) and resolves them to the full canonical ID (\`f61f-7e0a-36d3-4e7d\`) for subcommands such as \`ticket show\` and \`ticket exists\`. The 8-char prefix is the form shown in user-facing listings (e.g. \`list-epics\` output groups them as \`f61f-7e0a\\tP*\\t<title>\`), and other subcommands (\`list-epics\`, \`transition\`, \`comment\`) appear to accept it. Consistent prefix resolution is implied by the \`ticket list-epics\` UX, the orchestrator's documented use of 8-char IDs throughout sprint Phase 1, and the way the sprint skill instructs users to \"Enter the number or epic ID to execute.\"
Running \`.claude/scripts/dso ticket show f61f-7e0a\` exits 1 with:
Error: ticket \"f61f-7e0a\" has no CREATE or SNAPSHOT event
\`.claude/scripts/dso ticket exists f61f-7e0a\` also exits 1 (no stdout). Both succeed when called with the full ID \`f61f-7e0a-36d3-4e7d\`.
2. Sprint Phase 1 validation ran \`.claude/scripts/dso ticket show f61f-7e0a\` -> exit 1 with the error above.

content.text: * **merge strategy:** GitHub squash merge (single-parent merge commit)

Step 12 of /dso:end-session should detect that the worktree branch was already merged and skip running merge-to-main.sh. The skill documents three fallback checks: (1) git merge-base --is-ancestor, (2) commit-message grep for "(merge $BRANCH)", (3) git fetch + retry merge-base.
When a PR is merged via GitHub squash merge, the resulting merge commit on main has a single parent (not the worktree branch tip). As a result:
1. git merge-base --is-ancestor <branch> main → exits non-zero (branch is not an ancestor)
2. git log main --grep="(merge <branch>)" → finds no commit (squash commit title doesn't include that pattern)
3. git fetch + retry merge-base → still exits non-zero

All three is_merged checks fail even though gh pr view --json state returns {"state":"MERGED"}. If end-session were to run Step 11 after this, it would see 81 "unmerged" commits and invoke merge-to-main.sh on an already-merged branch, likely creating a duplicate PR or failing with a branch conflict.

In the session where this was discovered (epic ac1b-5e35, PR #96), the issue was noticed manually and merge-to-main.sh was correctly skipped. But the end-session skill has no code path that handles this case.
- PR #96 was squash-merged externally by the user after 3 CI llm-review failures
- end-session Step 12 ran: merge-base check returned NOT_MERGED despite PR state=MERGED
- Manually confirmed via gh pr view 96 --json state,mergeCommit that the PR was merged
- Skipped merge-to-main.sh invocation manually to avoid re-merge
- plugins/dso/skills/end-session/SKILL.md Step 11 (merge skip condition) and Step 12 (is_merged check)

- Fix: add a fourth fallback in the is_merged block that calls `gh pr list --head <branch> --state merged --json number` or `gh pr view --json state` to check GitHub's authoritative merge state before concluding NOT MERGED

content.text: On CI re-review (cycle ≥ 2), DSO_REVIEW_CYCLE should be set to 2+ so runner.py calls _fetch_pr_defenses() to suppress already-defended findings. The mirror-defenses-to-pr.sh CI job should post DEFENSE_RECORD comments from reviewer-findings.json to the PR.
Three root causes discovered during epic ac1b-5e35 PR #96 CI failures:

1. sprint-story-review.yml never sets DSO_REVIEW_CYCLE env var, so it always defaults to 1 in runner.py (line: `cycle_number = int(os.environ.get("DSO_REVIEW_CYCLE", "1"))`). Defense suppression is never active across retry runs.
2. mirror-defenses-to-pr.sh CI job reads from stdin with nothing piped — it is a no-op in CI. Manually posting DEFENSE_RECORD comments to the PR has no effect because the CI job never reads them.

3. Strategy E cluster-split (triggers at 400 LOC / 15 files) causes cross-cluster false positives: the CLAUDE.md cluster reviewer cannot see skills/ cluster to verify a skill file exists; the tests/ cluster reviewer cannot see the SKILL.md it tests.

Result: The defense mechanism is architecturally non-functional in CI. Each re-review run behaves as a fresh cycle 1 review with no memory of previous defenses, producing non-deterministic findings. PR #96 required 3+ CI runs and ultimately user-forced merge.
- Three CI llm-review runs on PR #96 (epic ac1b-5e35), each producing different blocking findings
- Attempted adding REVIEW-DEFENSE comments to source files — backfired (drew more attention)
- Attempted posting DEFENSE_RECORD comments to PR manually — had no effect (CI job is no-op)
- Escalated to user; user force-merged PR externally

content.text: # Pilot Anthropic advisor tool in DSO sub-agent dispatch
Placeholder epic to evaluate the advisor tool for cost/quality improvements in DSO's sub-agent architecture.

The advisor tool pairs a faster executor model (sonnet) with a higher-intelligence advisor (opus 4.7) consulted mid-generation via a server-side sub-inference. No nested Task call required — the advisor sees the executor's full transcript automatically.
- **Throttle relief.** When `orchestration.max_agents` tiers fire (90%/95% usage), every opus sub-agent we can downshift to sonnet helps.

- **Bypasses nesting prohibition (CLAUDE.md rule 17).** Resolution sub-agents currently can't dispatch nested Task calls; advisor is a server-side sub-inference, not a Task call, so it gives resolution agents strategic consultation without violating the nesting rule that produced `[Tool result missing due to internal error]` failures.

- **Known coding-agent win pattern.** Anthropic's published benchmarks show meaningful gains for "sonnet executor + opus advisor" on long-horizon coding workloads — which is exactly what sprint task agents and fix-bug agents do.
- Sprint task sub-agents (long coding loops, batch-dispatched)
- Review resolution sub-agents (constrained by no-nesting rule today)
- brainstorm scrutiny pipeline stages (with care — impartial-reviewer roles must stay as dedicated named agents per existing feedback)

- Beta header `advisor-tool-2026-03-01` required. Available on Claude API and Claude Platform on AWS only — NOT on Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry. Gate any rollout on consumer deployment surface.
- Supported pair we'd use: sonnet-4-6 executor + opus-4-7 advisor.

- Adds ~1.4–1.8k opus tokens per advisor call (including thinking, which is dropped before result returns). Cost story works only when it enables an executor downshift AND/OR reduces total tool-calls.
- `caching: ephemeral` on the tool definition pays off at ≥3 advisor calls per conversation. Enable for sprint long-loop agents; leave off for short fix-bug runs.

- Suggested system-prompt blocks from the docs are worth lifting: timing guidance (call before substantive work, before declaring done, when stuck) and conciseness instruction (sub-100 words, enumerated steps) cut advisor output ~35–45% in their evals.
1. **Known constraint cleanly bypassed.** CLAUDE.md rule 17 forbids resolution agents from nesting Task calls. Advisor sidesteps this without introducing new architectural risk.

2. **Failure cost is concrete.** Failed resolution attempts burn `review.max_resolution_attempts` (default 5) and then escalate to the user. Improving per-attempt success rate has measurable, observable impact.
3. **Scoped blast radius.** Single dispatch site (`plugins/dso/docs/workflows/prompts/review-fix-dispatch.md`); easy to A/B by toggling the tool definition.
4. **Existing telemetry.** DefenseStore records resolution outcomes per attempt — we already track what we'd need to measure.
- Resolution success rate per attempt (vs. baseline from recent sprints)
- Token cost per resolution (advisor adds opus tokens; only worthwhile if attempts drop)
### Open questions for stories under this epic
- How do we toggle the advisor tool on a single sub-agent dispatch path without coupling it to other agents?
- Where does the beta header get injected — sub-agent definition, dispatcher, or harness config?
- Do we need a `review.advisor_enabled` config knob, or always-on once validated?
- How do we measure "advice quality" beyond outcome metrics — sample-based human review of advisor responses?
- What's the rollback path if advisor responses degrade resolution quality (e.g., advisor pushes a sweeping refactor that resolution shouldn't attempt)?
## Out of scope for this epic
- Rolling advisor out to sprint task agents, fix-bug, or debug-everything. Those are follow-on epics gated on the pilot.
- Replacing existing opus-tier agents (reviewers, completion-verifier) — those are weak-fit by design.

P4 (backlog) — speculative cost/quality optimization on a beta-tagged tool. No user-visible problem driving urgency; revisit when (a) tool exits beta, or (b) we observe sustained throttling pain that this would relieve.

content.text: LLM reviewer specialists should ground claims in the actual file contents at the cited line range. False positives — claims of bugs that the cited code does not actually have — should be rare and not appear at `critical` / `fragile` severity. When the reviewer is unsure, it should reduce severity or omit the finding rather than fabricating evidence.

PR #98 cycle 2 (run 25751125173) llm-review produced 8 findings on a 233-line diff. Three of them (2 critical + 1 fragile, the highest-severity bucket) are demonstrably false based on the actual cited code. Two are stale from cycle 1 (claims already addressed by code or defense comment in the previous push).
**Example 1: critical false positive — fabricated control-flow gap.**
> Missing 'continue' statement after fail-closed logging on git ancestry check failure allows fall-through to record output, violates fail-closed trust boundary.

The actual cited block is a closed `if/elif/elif` chain. The first branch (`unexpected error`) emits a WARNING and ends. The other branches are not reachable when the first branch fires (per if/elif semantics). The block terminates with `fi` and the inline comment `# else: ... — exclude (silent)` documents the intended behavior. No 'fall-through to record output' is possible. The reviewer hallucinated the bug.
# else: QUERY_SHA is not in range and TIP is not its ancestor — exclude (silent)
**Example 2: critical false positive — bash idiom mis-read as defect.**
> Variable declaration ordering violation: exit codes shadowed by local declarations issued after assignment, rendering the fail-closed checks unreachable.

The actual pattern is the standard bash idiom: `local var; cmd && var=0 || var=$?`. Declaration on line 314 precedes assignment on line 315. Exit codes are captured correctly. Multiple existing tests rely on this pattern and pass GREEN. The reviewer mis-classified a standard idiom as a defect.
**Example 3: fragile false positive — fabricated missing-import claim.**
> Unresolvable import: deduplicate_region_findings function does not exist in dso_ci_review.findings module.

The function exists at `plugins/dso/scripts/dso_ci_review/findings.py`. The test file imports it with `# noqa: E402` and ALL 11 tests in the file pass when run locally. The reviewer fabricated a missing symbol that is present.
**Example 4: cycle-stale finding — defense comment not consumed.**

Cycle 1 finding 1 (secrets-as-env-vars) was defended via a PR issue comment with cross-workflow justification (same pattern as ci.yml). Cycle 2 finding 5 is the identical finding restated with no acknowledgement of the defense. The reviewer either does not read prior PR comments, or the prior-defenses-path artifact (`DSO_CI_REVIEW_PRIOR_DEFENSES_PATH`) is not populated for session→main PR llm-review runs. This is closely related to bug d565-805a (review cascade non-convergence), but the surface here is reviewer-prompt-level rather than orchestration-level.
1. Pushed commit 4c154d1b addressing PR #98 cycle 1 finding 3 (asymmetric fail-open). Defense comment posted on PR for findings 1/2/4.
2. Cycle 2 ran on the new HEAD. Reviewer produced 8 findings, including the 3 false positives + 2 cycle-stale findings detailed above.
3. Verified each by reading the actual cited code; documented in this ticket.
* Reviewer specialists: agents/dso:code-reviewer-light, dso:code-reviewer-security-red-team (and possibly others dispatched by the runner)
(a) Reviewer prompts do not require quoting the exact cited line range from the source file; reviewer is free to paraphrase or invent
(b) Reviewer is dispatched without the surrounding context window (only the diff hunk); can fabricate control-flow claims when the hunk includes only part of an if/elif chain
(c) No 'evidence grounding' verifier reviews findings before they post — false positives reach the PR
(d) Specialists do not see prior-cycle defense comments; same defended finding re-surfaces
1. Strengthen reviewer prompts: REQUIRE `cited_excerpt` to be a literal substring of the file at the cited line range; emit `UNGROUNDED` if the excerpt cannot be produced
2. Add a post-review verifier sub-agent that re-reads the cited lines and downgrades findings whose claims contradict the actual code
3. Wire the prior-defenses-path artifact for session→main PR runs (not just story branches)
4. Calibrate severity: `critical` / `fragile` should require not just a stated bug but a reachability proof or test that demonstrates exploitability
* Related: bug d565-805a (cascade non-convergence), bug 1348-f163 (CI review gate prior bypass)
* Out of scope: fixing PR #98 itself; this bug is to PREVENT future hallucinated findings, not to address the current PR.

STALE RED MARKER: tests/review/test-defense-store-sha-range.sh (marker: test_defense_store_write_records_sha_fields) — all RED-zone tests passed
To remove: sed -i.bak 's/ \[test_defense_store_write_records_sha_fields\]//' .test-index && rm .test-index.bak && git add .test-index
Test status recorded: failed — failed tests: ...[stale-red-marker:test_defense_store_write_records_sha_fields]

content.text: * **scope:** agent-facing display conventions in skill outputs, ticket CLI responses, commit messages, and PR comments
* **affected outputs:** /dso:sprint, /dso:end-session, /dso:fix-bug, /dso:create-bug, /dso:brainstorm Phase outputs; commit messages; user-facing summaries

When a ticket has multiple identifiers — short hex (`4ec9-cdb2`), human-friendly alias (`slid-opera-cabin`), Jira ID (`jira-dig-1647`) — agent-facing output should prefer the most human-readable form in the user's display:

1. If a Jira ID exists (i.e., the ticket is mirrored to Jira), prefer the Jira ID — it is the system-of-record identifier for cross-tool reference (PRs, dashboards, oncall, stakeholder communication).
2. Otherwise, prefer the alias (`slid-opera-cabin`) — easier to recall, less error-prone to retype, and unambiguous within DSO.
3. Use the short hex ID only as a fallback when neither of the above is available, or in machine-readable contexts (state files, JSON payloads, automation scripts).
The ticket CLI `create` command already emits both: `Created ticket slid-opera-cabin (4ec9-cdb2-b117-4f1c): ...`. The display path should honor that ordering.

This session (2026-05-12 f61f-7e0a-36d3-4e7d remediation) demonstrated the issue extensively. The agent (Claude Code as /dso:sprint orchestrator) consistently displayed short hex IDs in every user-facing surface:
* User-facing summary tables: `| Compliance-verifier .skipped requirement | 9780-b0d7 | filing |`
* PR comments: `commit 4c154d1b addressing PR #98 cycle 1 finding 3`
* AskUserQuestion option descriptions: `File bug for missing _LLM_DISPATCH_CMD`
* Bug ticket bodies referencing related bugs: `Related: bug d565-805a (cascade non-convergence)`
In each case, the alias (e.g. `drip-bay-blink`) and the Jira ID (when present) were available in the same response context but were not used.
1. Across ~16 bug tickets filed in this session, every reference was to the short hex ID.
2. User explicitly flagged this practice and asked for a bug ticket including the agent's own rationalization.
### Agent's rationalization for using short hex IDs in this session
When pressed, the rationalizations I (the agent) used were:

1. **Canonical / machine-readable form**: Short hex IDs are the canonical identifier in `.tickets-tracker/` event filenames, ticket CLI subcommand arguments, and shim invocations. Treating them as the universal display form felt 'safe.'

2. **Mental anchor consistency**: Cross-referencing IDs across PR comments, commit messages, and ticket bodies felt more reliable when one form was used throughout. Mixing aliases + hex IDs felt like it could introduce parsing/copy-paste errors for downstream readers.
3. **CLAUDE.md and skill files use hex IDs as examples**: `Bug fadc-6b5d`, `bug 8988-91be`, `(7c45-ee60)` — the project's own documentation models the convention I copied.

4. **Hex IDs are stable**: Aliases are auto-generated and theoretically more likely to be regenerated or change; hex IDs are SHA-derived and stable across migrations. This concern is largely hypothetical — aliases are stored alongside hex IDs in the event log.
5. **Length**: Hex IDs are shorter on the page than 3-word aliases (`4ec9-cdb2` vs `slid-opera-cabin`), so they fit more compactly in tables and bullet lists.
None of these rationalizations holds up under scrutiny for human-facing display:
* (1) is about the machine layer, not the human layer. The CLI emits both — the human-facing form is the alias.
* (2) is solved by always-display-alias-or-jira; consistency is preserved across the user-facing column.
* (3) is a self-perpetuating convention in skill files — those files are part of the bug surface (skill prose should also model alias-or-jira preference).
* (4) is hypothetical and not borne out by the .tickets-tracker schema.
* (5) is real but minor; aliases are typically 13-18 characters, hex IDs 9-19 characters with the long form. Compactness gain is small and human-readability loss is large.
* Affected hooks: pre-commit-compliance-verifier (commit message linter), check-sprint-trailer (trailer parser)
* Affected docs: CLAUDE.md (uses hex IDs throughout), all skill files (model the convention), bug-report-template.md
1. Skill files prose: when referring to ticket IDs in user-facing output, instruct agents to prefer Jira ID > alias > hex (in that order). Add a single-line rule near the top of every skill.
2. CLAUDE.md: add a section under 'Always Do These' specifying the preference order for ticket ID display.

3. `ticket show` and `ticket list` output schemas: ensure alias and jira_id fields are always returned at the top of the JSON; consumers (scripts, agents) read the preferred form from a single canonical field.
4. Optional: extend the bug-report-template to model the preference (currently models hex via `[Component]: [Condition] -> [Observed Result]` examples).
5. The `Closes <id>` git trailer convention should accept either form — the parser already does.
* Internal automation scripts and event files: hex IDs are correct (machine layer).
* Commit message bodies: aliases / Jira IDs are preferred but hex IDs should still be allowed (the parser must accept all forms).
* Bug ticket TITLES (because they appear in lists): aliases preferred.

content.text: PR-FINALIZE-WORKFLOW.md states: 'Always explicitly resolve the thread after addressing it — do NOT rely on GitHub auto-resolving from line changes.' The agent uses `gh api graphql ... resolveReviewThread` on each thread ID. This presumes findings are posted as PR REVIEW THREADS attached to specific file:line ranges, not as issue comments on the PR body.

Sessions 2026-05-12 cycles 1+2 on PR #98. llm-review posts each finding via the GitHub Issues API (`gh api repos/.../issues/<num>/comments`) instead of the Pull Request Reviews API (`gh api repos/.../pulls/<num>/reviews` with `comments[]` attached to file:line). Observed via:
gh api repos/navapbc/digital-service-orchestra/issues/98/comments -> 4 findings posted as issue comments (with markdown headers like '## DSO llm-review — finding 1/4')
1. PR-FINALIZE-WORKFLOW.md thread-resolution path is not exercisable — there ARE no threads to resolve.
2. pr-finalize-classify.sh sees the failing check (correct) but cannot surface structured `THREADS_UNRESOLVED` payload, only `CHECKS_FAILED`.
3. Defenses posted via `gh pr comment` also land as issue comments — no thread to mark resolved.
4. Future review cycles cannot distinguish defended vs new findings without parsing markdown content.
* Related: bug d565-805a (review cascade non-convergence) — this is one mechanism that causes the cascade

* Fix sketch: switch the llm-review GitHub poster to post via the Pull Request Reviews API with comments anchored to file:path:line. This produces real review threads. PR-FINALIZE-WORKFLOW.md and pr-finalize-classify.sh then operate as designed (parse threads, resolve threads, classify THREADS_UNRESOLVED).

content.text: * **observed in:** host project (downstream consumer) following plugin install from marketplace

The DSO plugin should NOT require host projects to commit a hardcoded absolute path containing one specific developer's home directory username. Claude Code provides a per-runtime variable for plugin root resolution (e.g. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` or marketplace cache path discovery). The shim and plugin scripts should resolve plugin_root via that variable, with the config key serving only as an optional override.
Multi-developer projects should be able to clone the repo and have the plugin Just Work without anyone needing to edit dso-config.conf.
A second developer (nataliewatkins) cloned a host project where dso-config.conf had been committed with:

The shim resolved plugin_root from this config key and looked for plugin scripts under the FIRST developer's home directory. Any `.claude/scripts/dso ...` invocation failed silently or with confusing errors. Diagnostic surface in the host project:

I can't list epics: the ticket store lives on a remote tickets branch and git fetch origin tickets fails with could not read Username for 'https://github.com' — git has no credential helper or auth configured for the remote.

1. Config path is stale. .claude/dso-config.conf has dso.plugin_root=/Users/joeoakhart/..., but the dso plugin you just installed lives under /Users/nataliewatkins/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/digital-service-orchestra/plugins/dso.

Workaround required editing dso-config.conf to substitute the second developer's username. This change cannot be committed back without breaking the first developer; each developer must keep a local-only override in their working tree (untracked or git-ignored). The config layer offers no host-machine-relative resolution.
1. Second developer cloned the host project repo.
2. `/dso:onboarding` or first `.claude/scripts/dso ticket` invocation failed because the shim's plugin_root resolution returned a path under the FIRST developer's home directory.
4. Secondary issue surfaced after the path fix: `ticket init` ran `git fetch origin tickets` and failed because https credentials were not configured (separate concern, not part of this bug).
* Affected scripts: shim `.claude/scripts/dso`, every plugin script invoked by the shim, every COMMIT-WORKFLOW.md / hook that sources ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}
* Affected skill: /dso:onboarding (initial project setup), /dso:init (host project configuration scaffolding)
* Anti-pattern: committing a per-developer absolute path to a shared config file.

1. Shim resolution order: (a) $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT env var if set, (b) detect marketplaces directory under $HOME/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/digital-service-orchestra/plugins/dso, (c) fall back to dso.plugin_root config key, (d) error with actionable message.
2. /dso:onboarding and /dso:init should NOT write an absolute dso.plugin_root to dso-config.conf — should rely on the env var / auto-discovery path.
- Remove the dso.plugin_root key entirely from dso-config.conf as a recommended default.
- Or document it as an OPTIONAL override and add it to .gitignore-recommended for the host project.
4. The shim error message when plugin_root cannot be resolved should explicitly mention the multi-developer scenario and the auto-discovery fallback.

The host project's session also surfaced a separate `xlator: command not found` error from a stop hook and a UserPromptSubmit hook — appears unrelated to plugin_root but indicates additional onboarding friction. Not in scope here.

The `git fetch origin tickets` HTTPS auth failure mentioned in the log is a separate onboarding concern (whether the plugin should prefer SSH for the tickets branch, or detect missing credentials more gracefully) — track as a distinct ticket if not already filed.

content.text: PR finalize loop converges. After fixing all blocking findings flagged in cycle N, cycle N+1 should either: (a) approve the PR (no blocking findings), (b) re-flag only the same findings (which then trigger same-failure escalation in PR-FINALIZE-WORKFLOW.md), or (c) flag a smaller subset. The DefenseStore protocol (prior-defenses-path) is intended to suppress already-defended findings.
PR #98 cycle 1 → 1 critical + 3 important (4 findings). User addressed the 1 legitimate finding (Trust boundary) + posted defense comments for the 3 defensible ones.
PR #98 cycle 2 (run 25751125173) after addressing cycle 1: **2 critical + 1 fragile + 5 important = 8 findings**. NEW findings include:
- (false positive) finding 2: claims deduplicate_region_findings does not exist — test passes locally with the same import
- (new surface) finding 4: artifact name injection via branch newlines — only theoretically reachable
- (stale) finding 5: secrets-as-env-vars — same finding as cycle 1; defense comment was posted but not consumed
- (new) findings 6/7: test coverage gaps in the tests just added
- (new) finding 8: documentation gap on the asymmetric logic (now removed — the finding is stale)
Cycle 2 introduced MORE blocking findings than cycle 1. Pattern is divergence rather than convergence.
1. Pushed commit 4c154d1b addressing cycle 1 finding 3 + posted defense for findings 1/2/4 as PR comment.
2. Cycle 2 ran (run 25751125173) — found 8 findings, half of which target the test/fix from step 1 + half of which restate / reframe earlier findings (with the defense comment not consumed).
3. Pattern matches existing bug 1348-f163 surface (CI review gate fail mode) but distinct: that's about bypass; this is about non-convergence.
* Workflow: PR-FINALIZE-WORKFLOW.md (bounded loop: same-failure 3x, per-PR max 15)
(a) prior-defenses-path artifact not produced on session→main PRs (it's a different workflow than sprint-story-review.yml)
(b) DefenseStore not consulted when llm-review runs on the session→main PR (only consulted on story branches per epic f61f-7e0a design)
(c) issue-comment-based defense is not machine-readable by the next review cycle; only resolved review THREADS suppress findings
(d) reviewer prompts encourage broader scope-expansion per cycle

* Fix sketch: investigate which DefenseStore wiring runs on the session→main PR llm-review job. The epic f61f-7e0a-36d3-4e7d design was per-story attestation; the session→main PR likely uses a different defense path (or none). If no defense path exists for the session-PR cycle, the reviewer will keep finding new surface every push.

content.text: * **Context Scope:** Host project bootstrapped via `platform` CLI as a Ruby on Rails application. Working directory is the host project root.
`plugins/dso/scripts/detect-stack.sh` documents the following root-level priority order in its header (lines 19–26):
5. ruby-rails      (Gemfile + config/routes.rb) — takes priority over ruby-jekyll

For a Ruby on Rails project, the documented contract for `ruby-rails` (line 14) is: *\"Gemfile (non-empty) AND config/routes.rb found.\"* When both markers are present, the script should output `ruby-rails`. The Python/Node priority comment (lines 28–31) explicitly justifies python-poetry winning over node-npm because *\"many Python projects include package.json for frontend tooling\"* — the same rationale applies to modern Rails (jsbundling-rails, importmap-rails, cssbundling-rails) and to projects scaffolded by the platform CLI, which install a root-level `package.json` alongside the Rails app.
In a host project created by `platform` CLI as a Rails app, `detect-stack.sh` returns:

Despite `Gemfile`, `config/routes.rb`, and a `package.json` all being present at the project root, the script short-circuits at the node-npm check (lines 87–92) and never reaches the ruby-rails check (lines 96–106). The ruby-rails detection rule is therefore unreachable for any Rails project that ships a root-level `package.json` — which is the default for platform-CLI-bootstrapped Rails projects, Rails 7 `jsbundling-rails`, and `cssbundling-rails`.
* Ran `bash plugins/dso/scripts/detect-stack.sh <host-project-root>` in a host Rails project created via platform CLI.

* **Known Workarounds:** Callers can override the detected stack via the consuming-script's stack-override mechanism (if any) or by manually invoking ruby-rails tooling; no in-script workaround exists short of patching the priority order.
* **Active Workflow:** Host-project stack detection (called by any DSO workflow that branches on project type)

content.text: * **Context Scope:** `plugins/dso/skills/onboarding/SKILL.md` — Phase 2 (Socratic dialogue), sections 8 (Jira) and 14 (Ticket prefix)
Before `/dso:onboarding` asks the user a configuration question that depends on understanding the DSO ticket system, the skill should present a short overview that establishes:

1. **What the DSO ticket system is** — a per-repo, event-sourced ticket tracker stored in an orphan `tickets` git branch under `.tickets-tracker/` (see `plugins/dso/docs/ticket-cli-reference.md` and CLAUDE.md "Architecture (pointers)" section).

2. **How DSO tickets relate to Jira** — DSO tickets are the source of truth in-repo; the Jira Bridge optionally mirrors them bidirectionally to a Jira project (one-way sync if Jira is read-only). Jira is not required; many projects run on DSO tickets alone.
3. **What a ticket prefix is for** — a short uppercase code that prefixes ticket aliases for human-readable identifiers (it is NOT the Jira project key; Jira sync uses `jira.project` separately).

The overview should appear once at the start of Phase 2 (or immediately before section 8), so that sections 8 (\"Does this project use Jira for issue tracking? If so, what's the Jira project key?\") and 14 (\"I'll use ticket prefix 'MA' for this project\") are askable from a position of informed consent.

This mirrors the contract pattern `/dso:onboarding` already uses for other features: section 9 (Figma) explains \"design.figma_collaboration — enables Figma design integration. Your Figma token stays as an env var\" *before* asking the yes/no. Sections 8 and 14 lack the equivalent framing for the larger and more novel ticket-system context.
Phase 2 of the onboarding skill jumps straight into ticket-system-related prompts without any prior framing:

* **SKILL.md line 640** (section 8): the user is asked `Does this project use Jira for issue tracking? If so, what's the Jira project key (e.g., \"MYAPP\" or \"DSO\")?` with one trailing note about credentials staying as env vars — but no explanation of what \"DSO syncing tickets\" means, whether DSO has its own ticket system, or what the user is opting in/out of.

* **SKILL.md lines 744–746** (section 14): the user is told `I'll use ticket prefix \"MA\" for this project (derived from \"my-app\"). Does that work, or would you prefer a different prefix?` with no statement that DSO maintains a per-repo ticket system, that this prefix scopes the in-repo system (not Jira), or where the resulting tickets will live (`.tickets-tracker/`, orphan `tickets` branch).
A user encountering these prompts cold cannot make a well-informed decision:
* They may decline the Jira prompt assuming \"DSO tickets\" are the same as Jira issues, when they are actually a distinct system that runs locally regardless of the Jira answer.
* They may pick a poor prefix (or confuse it with the Jira project key) because no explanation is given that the prefix is for DSO's own ticket alias scheme.

* They may not realize the orphan `tickets` branch and `.tickets-tracker/` directory will be created in later phases (Phase 3, lines 1200+), since no overview has connected sections 8 and 14 to the ticket-system initialization that follows.
* Inspected `plugins/dso/skills/onboarding/SKILL.md` Phase 2 section 14 (Ticket prefix confirmation, lines 733–747).

* Searched the file for any prior introduction of the DSO ticket system in Phase 0 or Phase 1: the only ticket-system mention before section 8 is a procedural note at line 244 (\"ticket system init and hook install both require git\"), which is a skip rule, not user-facing context.

* Section 8 prompt text: only one trailing note (\"credentials stay as environment variables — only the project key goes in config\"); no overview of DSO's own ticket system or how Jira interacts with it.
* Section 14 prompt text: derives a prefix from the project name and asks for confirmation; no statement of what the prefix scopes.

* **Known Workarounds:** Users who ask \"what is DSO ticket prefix for?\" or \"do I need Jira to use DSO?\" mid-onboarding will get an explanation from the running agent, but this requires the user to know enough to ask. No in-skill workaround.
* **Skills Invoked:** `plugins/dso/skills/onboarding/SKILL.md` — sections 8, 14, and the Phase 2 Gate (line 752+)

The cleanest fix is likely a short Phase-2 preamble (or a new section between 7 and 8) that introduces the DSO ticket system in 3–5 sentences before section 8 fires. Suggested content shape: \"DSO ships with its own in-repo ticket tracker (orphan `tickets` branch, `.tickets-tracker/`). It runs on every project that uses DSO and does not require Jira. The next two prompts (Jira project key, ticket prefix) configure how DSO's tickets sync outbound to Jira (optional) and how they appear locally (always).\"

content.text: * **Active Configs:** none required to reproduce — the trigger is the project state (blank repo) and the workflow path (Phase 1.5 → 1.6a nava-platform → 1.7)

When a user runs `/dso:onboarding` on a blank repo and uses the platform CLI (Phase 1.6a, `nava-platform` install) to scaffold a new app, the onboarding workflow should still ask the **project-specific design questions** that are documented in `SKILL.md` Phase 2 section 6 (lines 595–622):
* \"In one sentence, what is the specific value this UI delivers to the user?\" (vision — line 610)
* \"Describe 2–3 user archetypes — not just demographics, but behaviors.\" (user archetypes — line 612)
* Golden paths, visual language, accessibility targets (continued in lines 614–620)

These are inherently project-specific answers — a template registry cannot pre-supply them, because the registry does not know what the user's product is or who its users are. Phase 3 line 1482 explicitly states that `design-notes.md` is written for *\"UI projects only: vision, archetypes, golden paths, visual language, accessibility\"* — so the workflow's own downstream contract requires those answers to have been collected.
Phase 1.7's skip rationale at `phases/1.7-post-install-redetection.md` line 84 lists only the dimensions the registry **can** pre-answer:
> \"Templates pre-answer the Socratic dialogue questions (**stack, commands, architecture, CI, enforcement**) via the registry metadata and installed project structure.\"
Design (and the project-specific design subquestions) is absent from that list. The skip should therefore preserve the design section of Phase 2, not skip it.
`phases/1.7-post-install-redetection.md` Step 5 (lines 84–104) skips **all** of Phase 2, not just the registry-derivable dimensions:
# Portable in-place delete — works on BSD and GNU sed
> \"Do NOT ask the user any Socratic dialogue questions from Phase C. Proceed directly to Phase D.\"
The user receives this banner instead:
Skipping project dialogue (template pre-configured) — proceeding directly to DSO infrastructure setup.
Net effect on the blank-repo + platform-CLI path:
* Section 6 design questions (vision, archetypes, golden paths, visual language, accessibility) — **never asked**.
* The downstream artifact `design-notes.md` (Phase 3, line 1482) — either written with empty/placeholder content for these fields or skipped entirely.
* The `design` confidence (line 146 of SKILL.md: `medium` if `package.json` has a UI framework reference, `low` otherwise) — overridden by the blanket Phase-2 skip regardless of confidence level.

This regression is specific to the **template-install** branch (Phases 1.5 → 1.6a/1.6b → 1.7). When the user declines templates in Phase 1.5 (or the install fails and the manual flow is selected), Phase 1.7 is skipped and Phase 2 runs normally — so the bug only affects the platform-CLI new-app path.

* Read `plugins/dso/skills/onboarding/SKILL.md` lines 1476–1482 (phase summary table — confirms Phase 1.7 \"skip Phase 2 entirely\" and Phase 3 \"design-notes.md (UI projects only: vision, archetypes, ...)\")
* Phase 1.7 Step 5 unconditionally deletes the `Phase 2: Socratic Dialogue Loop` entry from PHASE_PLAN.
* Phase 1.7 Step 6 explicitly notifies the user that the dialogue is being skipped.
* The skip rationale's enumerated dimensions (stack, commands, architecture, CI, enforcement) do not include design.
* User can decline the Phase 1.5 template menu (option 0) to force Phase 2 to run, but this defeats the purpose of using the platform CLI for scaffolding.
* User can manually edit `.claude/design-notes.md` post-onboarding to add vision/archetype content.
* Both workarounds are inefficient compared to the expected in-workflow prompt.
* **Active Workflow:** `/dso:onboarding` Phase 1.7 (Post-Install Re-Detection) and the Phase 2 skip it triggers

Suggested fix shape (not part of the report; for triage convenience): scope Phase 1.7's Phase-2 skip to the registry-derivable sections (stack, commands, architecture, CI, enforcement) and keep Phase 2 sections 4 (infrastructure) and 6 (design) — running just those two sections preserves the project-specific discovery while still honoring the \"template pre-configured\" rationale for the rest.
